parts: A job application is a formal letter to a possible employer applying for a specific post. It accompanies a résumé or CV (bio-data) and highlights your qualifications and interest.

Structure: sender's information (name, address, phone, e-mail), date, employer's information (name, title, company, address), salutation ('Dear Hiring Manager' if the name is unknown), opening paragraph (the post and where you saw it), middle paragraph(s) (qualifications and skills matched to the job, with achievements), closing paragraph (enthusiasm, résumé attached, request for an interview), complimentary close and signature.

Tips: tailor each application to the job; keep it to one page; stress education if you lack experience; show skills from projects, clubs, volunteering and sports (teamwork, leadership, communication, time management); be positive, not apologetic; format neatly and proofread.

A CV ('course of life') is a full, detailed record of education, career, publications, awards and so on — British in style, used in academics and research, with no page limit. A résumé (American in style) is a short summary of one to two pages, tailored to each job, often in bullet points. Most companies now prefer résumés, which are easier to screen.

A good résumé is attractive, well-organised, easy to read and free of errors. Common headings: heading (name, address, phone, e-mail — no date), personal details, employment objective, education (most recent first), employment experience (most recent first), special skills and activities, references. List the stronger of education and experience first.

A cover (covering) letter goes before the résumé. It is a 'sales letter' that must catch the reader's attention favourably, convince him or her that you are qualified, and request an interview. Identify the post and how you heard of it, summarise your qualifications and refer to the résumé, and say where and when you can be reached.
